form.current-chamber: IN THE SENATE OF THE UNITED STATES

action.action-desc: Mr. Tillis (for himself, Mr. Moran, Mr. Cramer, Mr. Cotton, Mr. Perdue, and Mr. Rounds) introduced the following bill; which was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs

form.official-title: To require the Securities and Exchange Commission and certain Federal agencies to carry out a study relating to accounting standards, and for other purposes.

section.text: This Act may be cited as the Continued Encouragement for Consumer Lending Act.

paragraph.text: the term appropriate committees of Congress means—

subparagraph.text: the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs of the Senate; and
the Committee on Financial Services of the House of Representatives;

paragraph.text: the term CECL means the accounting standard in Accounting Standards Update 2016–13, Financial Instruments—Credit Losses (Topic 326), issued by the Financial Accounting Standards Board in June 2016, as amended by Accounting Standards Update 2018–19, Codification Improvements to Topic 326, Financial Instruments—Credit Losses, issued by the Financial Accounting Standards Board in November 2018;
the term Commission means the Securities and Exchange Commission;
the term Federal financial regulators means—

subparagraph.text: the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System;
the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection;
the Director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency; and
the National Credit Union Administration; and

paragraph.text: the term small business concern has the meaning given the term in section 3(a) of the Small Business Act (15 U.S.C. 632(a)).

subsection.text: The Commission and the Federal financial regulators, in consultation with the Financial Accounting Standards Board, shall conduct a quantitative study of—

paragraph.text: the potential impact that the implementation of CECL may have on the availability of credit, with a particular focus on the impact on that availability—

subparagraph.text: for consumers and small business concerns; and
with respect to the credit products on which consumers and small business concerns rely during periods of economic expansion and during recessions;
accelerate the depletion of regulatory capital that is available for lending purposes during a recession;
have a greater impact on regulatory capital, or extend the period in which regulatory capital is reduced, during a recession; or
pose any other systemic risks to the economy of the United States;

paragraph.text: the potentially disproportionate impact that the implementation of CECL may have on financial institutions, taking into account—

subparagraph.text: the various sizes and levels of complexity of those financial institutions; and
the different amounts of resources that are available to those financial institutions;

paragraph.text: the potential impact that the implementation of CECL may have on the decisions made by investors; and
the potential competitive impact that the implementation of CECL may have on institutions in the United States as a result of differing international accounting standards used to measure credit loss.

subsection.text: Not later than 1 year after the date of enactment of this Act, the Commission and the Federal financial regulators shall submit to the Financial Accounting Standards Board and the appropriate committees of Congress a report—

paragraph.text: regarding the results of the study conducted under subsection (a); and

subparagraph.text: the identification of any negative impacts resulting from the implementation of CECL; and
recommendations for changes to CECL to eliminate or mitigate the negative impacts described in subparagraph (A).

section.text: During the period beginning on the date of enactment of this Act and ending on the date that is 1 year after the date on which the Commission and the Federal financial regulators submit the report required under section 3(b), neither the Commission nor any of the Federal financial regulators may require a person to comply with CECL.
